items.originalTitle: Inside the battle to lead the RNC after its midterm wipeout
items.author: Aaron Pellish, Erin Doherty and Andrew Howard
items.title: Inside the battle to lead the RNC after its midterm wipeout
items.summary: The chair of the Republican National Committee is scrambling to avoid becoming the party’s midterms scapegoat. With President Donald Trump’s backing, Joe Gruters would normally be a lock to retain his position as RNC chair. But after this month’s brutal midterm losses, he is now trying to fend off an upstart and surprisingly strong challenge from co-chair KC Crosbie ahead of the January leadership election. As both candidates jockey behind the scenes for support, deep divisions have emerged between members over who bears responsibility for the wipeout earlier this month and what comes next. Party leaders have been reluctant to publicly point fingers at Trump and his unpopular agenda. Instead, conversations with more than two dozen RNC members and operatives familiar with the committee’s dynamics reveal that some are channeling their frustration toward Gruters. Even as his supporters argue he’s being unfairly blamed for a difficult political environment, Gruters could still become the fall guy. For some of Gruters’ critics, the decision is simple: Someone must pay for the once-unthinkable losses. “It is time for new leadership. That's nothing against Joe at all,” said Kentucky GOP Chair Robert Benvenuti, who plans to vote for Crosbie. “But different times require different leadership, different types of leaders.” An undecided RNC member added: “There's an awful lot of anger.” That member, granted anonymity to speak candidly about private conversations, described members questioning whether to “rubber stamp the guy that rightly or wrongly is seen as the architect of this mess.” The debate within the RNC — whether to break with the Trump-backed candidate or stick with the status quo — mirrors the broader reckoning underway in the GOP over how closely to align with the president moving forward. Many Republicans have resigned themselves to Trump’s continued dominance over the next two years, but some RNC members have already begun to agitate for change in other ways, including by calling for an autopsy of the midterms and for congressional leadership elections to be delayed. Several RNC members said Gruters helped the committee raise millions this cycle, arguing that alone is a key part of his job and he handled it well. Others were frustrated that the RNC didn’t engage or spend money in their states earlier. And some members criticized Gruters for allowing the RNC to become overly enmeshed in the White House’s political operation. “The party raised a lot of money, and we spent it. I don't think that there's a whole lot of that that can be laid at [Gruters’] feet,” said West Virginia GOP chair Josh Holstein, who said he has not yet committed either way in the leadership race. “At the same time, I know there's a lot of members of the committee that feel we need to go a different direction, and that the RNC needs to be a little more autonomous in its decision making.” The RNC and Crosbie declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Gruters campaign said in a statement that RNC members “are rallying behind Chairman Gruters because they know he will never stop fighting for Republicans.” “Chairman Joe Gruters has 25 years of experience at every level of the Republican Party, shattering fundraising records, building the largest election integrity operation in party history, and advancing President Trump’s agenda,” the campaign said. The outcome of the leadership race, which will be determined by a secret ballot, will test just how far RNC members are willing to go to change course — even if it means defying Trump. And the stakes are enormous, with the RNC playing a key role in the presidential race, including running the GOP primary debates, hosting the party’s 2028 convention and supporting the eventual nominee. Complicating the calculation is Trump’s own involvement: The president has been a vocal supporter of Gruters and has privately suggested that if Crosbie wins the leadership battle, he wouldn’t assist the RNC with fundraising ahead of 2028, according to two people familiar with the threat who were granted anonymity to speak about private details. The threat was first reported by Axios . It’s an apparent acknowledgement that even Trump knows it’s a real contest — and that his chosen candidate may become a scapegoat. Vice President JD Vance, who also serves as the RNC’s finance chair and is considering a presidential bid, has privately offered to assist Gruters’ reelection campaign, according to a person with direct knowledge of the outreach granted anonymity to speak about private details. Gruters has not yet taken Vance up on his offer, the person said. Vance’s office did not respond to a request for comment. “There is an element that is concerned about this underlying President Trump support, and if we don’t vote for his guy, we’re undermining the president and further giving him more bad news, black eyes, and there’s some sensitivities to that,” said a second RNC member who is undecided about the leadership election and granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive political dynamics. “But you also have some that are more protective of the brand and the party than they are to the person, especially given the results of this last election cycle,” the person said. Trump allies have been checking in with RNC members to gauge where they stand in the leadership race, said the RNC member, who received such a call. It’s not yet clear where the membership stands. Both Gruters’ and Crosbie’s camps are keeping their whip counts closely guarded in part to avoid a repeat of the 2022 RNC chair election, when allies seeking to oust former chair Ronna McDaniel aggressively badgered party members in hopes of elevating Harmeet Dhillon. “I think it's going to be a close race,” said Holstein, the West Virginia GOP chair. Behind the scenes, both candidates have been courting RNC members. Gruters has called people to solicit their support and leaned on both Trump’s endorsement and the consequences of Trump pulling out of future RNC fundraising. Rhode Island GOP Chair Allyn Meyers said Gruters sent him and the state’s other RNC members the president’s Truth Social post giving him his “complete and total endorsement.” “You don’t fire your best salesman because he’s got a bad quarter,” said Illinois GOP chair Bob Grogan, who plans to support Gruters. Crosbie, for her part, has sent a 10-12 page detailed survey to RNC members asking specific questions about the timing of when resources were deployed to their state this cycle and about staffing, among other areas, according to three people familiar with the survey. In conversations with undecided party members, Crosbie has pledged greater transparency into the party’s finances, one of the people said. She is also making her case to members who are frustrated by the party’s perhaps too close coordination with Trump world and want to have greater say in the RNC’s strategy. The RNC has historically operated as a political arm of the president whenever a Republican is in the White House. “You want the coordination, you want the closeness and the efficiency of it,” said Washington GOP chair Jim Walsh, who did not share who he’d be supporting in January. However, he added: “You want those two to be two different heads, two different brains, two different hearts, and you want a little tension there because you riff off each other on how you should proceed on a campaign or on a cycle strategy.” A national GOP strategist who supports Gruters pushed back on the calls for a more independent RNC. “This is not Model UN. It’s about winning elections,” said the person, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Whether they plan to vote for Gruters, Republican Party chairs from red and blue states alike told POLITICO the midterm results raise the need for a serious reckoning over the role the RNC should play in future cycles — and how it appeals to a broader swath of the electorate. “Regardless of who the chair is, I think there has to be changes in the way the committee operates,” said Ben Proto, Connecticut’s GOP chair, who did not share who he would be supporting in January. “The committee has to look beyond those, you know, in 2024, it was the seven states. In 2026, it was the highly targeted areas. I think we have to broaden our approach to the electorate. We have to look at 50 states.” “We took a pretty good beating two weeks ago or so,” said Benvenuti, of Kentucky. “And in my view, that should cause deep reflection about how the organization should be run, how messaging should be done, how the organization should function internally.” Lauren Fedor contributed reporting.

items.originalTitle: People Are Getting Worse at Handling Uncertainty
items.author: Veronique Greenwood
items.title: People Are Getting Worse at Handling Uncertainty
items.summary: —Photo-Ilustration by Chloe Dowling for TIME (Source Image: mariannehope/Getty Images) Living with the unknown isn’t always easy. Not knowing if layoffs are headed your way or whether you’ll be able to afford rent would be difficult for anyone. But when the pressure of the unknown becomes so intense it interferes with daily life, this “intolerance of uncertainty,” as psychologists call it, becomes a risk factor for mental-health disorders, primarily anxiety and depression. Now, in a paper in JAMA Psychiatry , psychologists find that this trait rose in North America from 1992 to 2023. Using data on college students in about 140 studies, the researchers found a gradual rise at first, then a steeper one starting around 2012. The results mirror increasing trends of symptoms of anxiety and depression among young people, suggesting that they are linked not just to rising awareness of mental illness but also to a change in our underlying ability to handle uncertainty about the future. How young people’s mental health has changed Rates of anxiety and depression in young people in the U.S. and the U.K. have been rising for some time , studies have found . Some researchers have suggested that increased awareness of mental-health disorders has contributed to increased diagnoses. Others have speculated that economic hardship or social media have played a role . “Some authors have argued that 2012 was an inflection point, in part because mobile phone technology became so widespread among young people in the early 2010s,” says Jeroen van Baar, an epidemiology researcher at Boston University School of Public Health and an author of the new paper. One idea is that smartphones insulate us from uncertainty , to some extent, by providing information on demand. Spending time on a smartphone can also be a coping strategy to deal with the discomfort of uncertainty, but might be only of limited reassurance in reality. While the hypothesis that phones are involved needs more investigation before it’s clear whether it explains the trend, he says, “what our paper adds to this discussion is that it's not just the anxious or depressive symptoms that change around that time. It's also this underlying process of intolerance of uncertainty.” A less-explored risk factor for anxiety Intolerance of uncertainty is assessed using questionnaires asking people to rate how much they relate to statements like “I can’t stand being taken by surprise” or “I always want to know what the future has in store for me.” Psychologist Mark Freeston of Newcastle University in the U.K., who was part of the group behind the first questionnaires, still remembers the conversation more than 30 years ago in Montreal when he and his colleagues discussed the idea that intolerance of uncertainty could be a vulnerability factor of its own. They were wondering about the cognitive underpinnings of generalized anxiety disorder. “Current wisdom at the time was that worry was problem solving gone wrong,” he says, “and we'd come to the conclusion that people with generalized anxiety disorder, dominated obviously by worry, knew how to solve problems.” They didn’t reach the point of acting on that knowledge, however, because they were overwhelmed by trying to cover every possible outcome, for instance. The concept went on to be used in a stream of studies over the next few decades. Psychologists and other researchers found that intolerance of uncertainty reflected an important aspect of mental health that transcends individual diagnoses. “Then the pandemic came along,” says Freeston, “and suddenly the rest of the world discovered that the world is not certain. As if it ever had been—but everyone was under the belief, particularly in first-world countries, at least, that people had control over their lives.” A new wave of research assessed how intolerance of uncertainty affected people’s health during a highly uncertain time. The new study does not cover the effects of the pandemic in detail, says van Baar. “We only have one, two, maybe three years of potential COVID effect in the data.” But work from other groups suggests that this period had a substantial impact on the mental health of young people in particular. Freeston, who was not involved in the new study, speculates that the rise it documents has to do with a different kind of change, one that started much earlier. “I don't actually believe that the world got objectively worse in a North American context at the time when you start seeing those increases,” he says. “I'm not convinced that the world certainly became more dangerous or more threatening. I think people had access to more information, and they relied less on their own [experience].” For his part, in future work, van Baar hopes to continue exploring how a natural human behavior—trying to predict what happens next, and suffering when accurate predictions are difficult—interacts with the features of the world we live in. “I think there are signs from macroeconomics, from geopolitics, and from other domains like the job market under AI and so on, that suggest that the world that young people grow up in today is quite uncertain, potentially more uncertain than it was, say, in the '90s. This is a contentious claim, but I think there's some evidence pointing toward that,” he says. How to live alongside uncertainty “One of the things that we learned during the pandemic is that you cannot ‘information’ your way out of uncertainty,” says Freeston. “As soon as you have more information, you haven't eliminated uncertainty. You've just moved what you're uncertain about.” That means more information can lead to a great sense of anxiety: Reassurance seems forever out of reach. He divides information into four categories, with the first being things you actually need to know today, like whether the grocery store is open and whether your flight is canceled . The second is information about the bigger picture behind current events, which you can get from journalists and experts but which will also bring some additional uncertainty to the table. “You may feel more informed, but you're less certain. It comes at a cost,” he says. “The third category of information is essentially probably the great majority of the digital world, and this is clickbait, it's hooks. This is people ostensibly providing information, but it's for their benefit. So it's not about you; it's about them…that is a category you really don't need,” he says. The fourth category is what he calls “rebalancing information”: the kind that’s closer to home or involves causes you’re close to. During the pandemic, he explored regional newspapers and found something interesting. “What you found if you looked at those news sources, even in the worst part of the pandemic, was the local petty criminals were still being petty criminals, and animals were still being rescued. Children were winning prizes. Charities were doing amazing things.” Consuming more information from this category—and less from people you don't know or trust online—may be one way to ground yourself in an unpredictable world. “I think one of the ways that we can dial down the impact of uncertainty is people becoming more selective in their use” of information, Freeston says.

The proposed rule changes would add two new parts to the regulations that govern the census: One change would remove a question about race and ethnicity, while another would add a citizenship question. Also among the proposed changes is a line that would formally bar questions about sexual orientation from being included. The US census is critical in understanding the American population. But this sweeping census rule change, quietly proposed by the Trump administration before the midterm elections, could reshape US society as we know it, warn some civil rights advocates.

items.originalTitle: The Holiday Tradition of Pretending Our Families Get Along Perfectly
items.author: Jillian Sanders
items.title: The Holiday Tradition of Pretending Our Families Get Along Perfectly
items.summary: —CSA-Printstock—Getty Images Imagine ending a romantic relationship after years of unresolved conflict. The arguments have become familiar, the resentments have accumulated, and conversations that once offered the possibility of understanding now go nowhere. Eventually, you accept that the relationship isn't working and decide to go your separate ways. Now imagine being told that you're still expected to spend the holidays together every year: to arrive with a gift, exchange pleasantries over dinner, smile together for photographs, and ask about each other's lives as though the years of conflict between you never existed. We would find this arrangement peculiar, unhealthy, even cruel, if it involved a former romantic partner. Yet when the person sitting across the table is a relative, we consider it perfectly normal. Hollywood has long reinforced this expectation through countless holiday movies in which dysfunctional families gather, dredge up old grievances , and somehow reconcile before the credits roll. From The Family Stone and Home for the Holidays to Four Christmases and This Christmas , these movies offer what real life so often doesn't: the promise that even the deepest family divisions can be healed. In reality, many families gather year after year without ever confronting the issues that divide them. They uphold traditions , exchange expressions of love, and maintain the appearance of togetherness, only to return to their strained relationships once the wreaths have come off the doors and the Christmas trees have been carried to the curb. But maintaining that illusion of perfect family harmony can come at a considerable emotional cost. According to a 2023 American Psychological Association survey , 43% of American adults said holiday stress interfered with their ability to enjoy the season. We often attribute that stress to money, travel, and competing obligations. But what about the pressure to pretend our family relationships are healthier than they actually are? A friend of mine, now in her late forties, has a complicated relationship with her older sister, in part because they experienced two entirely different childhoods. When their parents divorced, her sister was 17 and preparing to leave for college. My friend was just nine, left to navigate two households, custody arrangements, and the emotional aftermath of her parents' separation. While her older sister remembers a relatively stable upbringing, my friend recalls years of uncertainty and upheaval. As adults, their memories of family life are so different that conversations about their childhood often escalate into heated phone calls, followed by months of silence. For my friend, the most painful part is not that she and her sister remember their childhood differently, but that her sister, who was largely spared the upheaval of their parents’ divorce, has never fully acknowledged what her younger sibling endured. Because her sister never experienced the same instability, she seems unable to appreciate how profoundly those years shaped my friend’s life. The divide between them isn't simply a matter of conflicting memories. It's the frustration of having one's experiences dismissed by someone who wasn’t there to witness them. Perhaps it's not surprising, then, that a YouGov survey found that 24% of American adults are estranged from a sibling, with 18% of those saying they had simply grown apart. After all, growing up together doesn't guarantee that siblings will remain close, or that the bond they shared in childhood will endure into adulthood. Parents, meanwhile, are often caught in the middle. As they grow older, many grow weary of the disagreements between their adult children. Understandably, they want the holidays to be a time of peace and togetherness, not confrontation. But in their desire to preserve family traditions, they may unintentionally ask their children to set aside years of hurt that have never truly been resolved. A second friend in her mid-thirties described how her once-close relationship with her brother deteriorated after years of conflict with his wife. What began as occasional disagreements gradually drove a deep wedge between them, culminating in an argument in which her brother accused her of being unfair to his wife and dismissed her attempts to explain why she felt hurt. The argument was never resolved, and neither sibling has made an effort to reconnect. Nearly three years later, they no longer exchange birthday wishes or speak on the phone, though their mother continues to invite them both home for the holidays, hoping they might finally put the past behind them. She understands her mother’s longing for family togetherness and also mourns the bond she once shared with her brother. This friend says she resents the expectation that she should set aside years of unresolved hurt to preserve the illusion of family harmony. Of course, not all siblings who have grown apart stop speaking entirely. Some continue to exchange birthday cards, send presents to each other's children, and share holiday meals. But beneath those gestures of goodwill, the relationship may have become more about honoring a shared past than maintaining a connection in the present. These rituals may be a way of holding on to what remains when neither person quite knows how to bridge the distance between them. Another friend who is about the same age described a different kind of sibling distance, one rooted not in conflict but in a lack of closeness. She and her older sister never shared the kind of bond that made them confidantes growing up. Now living in different states, they keep in touch sporadically and see each other at family events, but rarely try to connect beyond those occasions. This third friend has made peace with the fact that she and her sister are fundamentally different people who might never have become friends had they not been related. While she cherishes her relationship with her nephews, she no longer believes that being sisters obliges them to be close. There can be freedom in accepting a relationship for what it is rather than what we think it ought to be. Not every strained sibling relationship requires a difficult conversation or a reckoning with the past. Sometimes people can acknowledge their differences, adjust their expectations, and move forward. But when years of resentment have accumulated, trust has been broken, or siblings remember the same childhood very differently, making peace may require more than simply agreeing to leave the past behind. We can spend years examining our behavior, confronting old wounds, and learning how to build healthier relationships. But what happens when the person we're trying to make peace with has no interest in doing the same? Even an offer to attend counseling together can go unanswered, leaving one sibling wondering whether reconciliation is possible when the other isn't willing to participate. Ultimately, we can take responsibility for our own mistakes, offer forgiveness, and leave the door open to reconciliation. But we cannot make someone else walk through it. Of course, family relationships are different from romantic ones. They are woven into the stories of who we are, the homes we grew up in, the parents who raised us, and the children who come after us. Creating distance from a sibling can mean losing far more than one relationship. It can mean missing a niece's birthday party, learning about a nephew's first day of school secondhand, or realizing you've become a stranger to children you once held as babies. Weddings become occasions for carefully arranged seating, and family celebrations become reminders of who's missing rather than opportunities to enjoy being together. Acknowledging these losses doesn't mean every fractured relationship can or should be repaired. But it does raise an important question: How do we continue to love our families without asking one another to ignore the realities of those relationships? The first step may be accepting that loving your family doesn't mean agreeing to every expectation that comes with being part of it. For some, that means attending Thanksgiving dinner but choosing not to stay overnight. For others, it means celebrating Christmas with their parents on a different day to avoid a strained sibling relationship, or declining a family gathering without being made to feel guilty. It may also mean maintaining a loving relationship with their parents without being expected to reconcile with a sibling. Rather than insisting that everyone celebrate together, families can ask what each person feels comfortable with, respect those boundaries, and find new ways to spend time together. The goal doesn't have to be recreating the holidays we remember. It can be making room for the family we are today, rather than the one we wish we still were. Maybe the greatest gift we can give one another this holiday season isn't another wrapped present or another carefully staged family photograph. Maybe it's the freedom to acknowledge that our relationships are complicated, that love doesn't erase years of hurt, and that sharing a holiday table isn't the same as sharing a close relationship. Because sometimes the hardest part of going home for the holidays isn't facing the people we've grown apart from. It's pretending we haven't grown apart.

items.originalTitle: A Guide to the 4 Caucuses That Could Shape the Democratic House
items.author: Nik Popli
items.title: A Guide to the 4 Caucuses That Could Shape the Democratic House
items.summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Speaker-designate, speaks alongside two other House Democratic leaders, Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, on Nov. 18, 2026, during a news conference at the Capitol in Washington, DC. —Saul Loeb—AFP via Getty Images Democrats are preparing to take control of the House of Representatives with a substantially larger majority and an influx of new members who cover every corner of the party’s “big tent. ” Incoming Democratic freshman include several democratic socialists and even more moderates who won in competitive and Republican-leaning districts. Many campaigned on lowering costs, improving health care, and providing a practical alternative to President Donald Trump. Some promised to fight for more sweeping changes to the country's economic and political systems. The competing priorities will be among the biggest challenges for Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the speaker-designate , who will be tasked with maintaining unity in a party whose leaders frequently celebrate its ideological diversity. Much of that debate will unfold within the House's major ideological and governing caucuses, which are preparing to welcome dozens of new members when Congress convenes in January. The two heavyweights are the centrist New Democrat Coalition—the largest caucus—and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, but the smaller Blue Dog Coalition and the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus could also prove influential as Democrats confront the limits of what they can accomplish with Trump in the White House and a Senate where most major legislation will still require Republican support. The new members will not necessarily divide neatly along ideological lines, and membership in the groups can overlap. But their growing ranks offer an early indication of where lawmakers may seek allies and how the party's internal balance of power could change. Here are the four caucuses to watch in the next Congress. New Democrat Coalition Rep. Nikki Budzinski, the chair of the New Democrat Coalition, attends a news conference with the group on Feb. 26, 2026, in Leesburg, Va. —Tom Williams—CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Estimated membership: 142 House Democrats Members in the new Congress: The coalition added 40 members, including about 30 Democrats who flipped Republican-held seats in the midterms. Its new members include Representatives-elect Amish Shah and JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona; Richard Pan, Jacqui Irwin, and Marni von Wilpert of California; Jessica Killin and Manny Rutinel of Colorado; Luke Bronin of Connecticut; Pia Dandiya of Florida; Christina Bohannan, Lindsay James, and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa; Donna Miller and Melissa Bean of Illinois; J.D. Ford of Indiana; Zach Dembo of Kentucky; Adrian Boafo of Maryland; Sean McCann, Christina Hines, and Jeremy Moss of Michigan; Jake Johnson of Minnesota; Fred Wellman of Missouri; Jamie Ager of North Carolina; Denise Powell of Nebraska; Stefany Shaheen of New Hampshire; Rebecca Bennett of New Jersey; Teresa Benitez-Thompson of Nevada; Cait Conley of New York; Kristina Knickerbocker of Ohio; Bob Harvie, Paige Cognetti, and Janelle Stelson of Pennsylvania; Nancy Lacore of South Carolina; Bobby Pulido and Johnny Garcia of Texas; Ben McAdams of Utah; Shannon Taylor and Elaine Luria of Virginia; and Mitchell Berman and Rebecca Cooke of Wisconsin. Leadership: Representative Nikki Budzinski of Illinois was elected as chairman for the next Congress. Other leaders include Representatives Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico, Kim Schrier of Washington, Greg Landsman of Ohio and Marilyn Strickland of Washington as vice chairs. Overview: With over 140 members, the New Democrat Coalition is not only the largest Democratic caucus, it is poised to represent more than half of the Democrats in the House. Its members, who sit at the party's center, generally favor pragmatic economic policies, private-sector growth and bipartisan compromise. Its expansion reflects the importance of moderate candidates to Democrats' electoral success in November. The coalition's growing membership could give it considerable influence over which bills reach the House floor, particularly as Jeffries seeks to demonstrate that the new Democratic majority can deliver results on the economic concerns that dominated the midterm campaign. Many of its incoming members represent competitive districts where voters may be skeptical of more expansive progressive proposals, giving them a strong political incentive to focus on measures that can attract broader support. Policy priorities: The group outlined its legislative ambitions in an Affordability Agenda released in February, which focuses on five major household expenses: health care, housing, energy, family care and everyday essentials such as groceries. Its proposals include extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, strengthening Medicare and Medicaid, restricting surprise medical billing and expanding prescription drug price protections. On housing, the coalition wants to ease permitting and zoning restrictions to help build four million new homes over the next decade. It has also called for a national paid family and medical leave program, expanded access to universal prekindergarten and measures to increase competition in the grocery industry. The coalition has placed particular emphasis on reversing Trump's tariffs, which its members argue have increased costs for consumers and businesses. Its agenda also calls for restoring congressional authority over trade policy and making it easier to build new energy infrastructure, including through changes to federal permitting requirements. What to watch: The coalition's influence could prove especially significant in debates over health care, where some moderates favor expanding existing programs rather than pursuing Medicare for All, and in negotiations over which pieces of legislation stand a realistic chance of becoming law. Congressional Progressive Caucus Rep. Greg Casar, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, speaks at a CPC press conference on Nov. 8, 2026, outside the US Capitol Building in Washington, DC. —Aaron Schwartz—Getty Images Estimated membership: 105+ House Democrats Overview: While the Squad gets more media attention , all of its members belong to the much larger Congressional Progressive Caucus, which more formally represents the party's left wing in the House. The CPC has long advocated policies including universal health care, stronger labor protections, immigration reform, climate action, and greater government intervention to address economic inequality. Jeffries, the Speaker-designate, is a former CPC member. Members in the new Congress : Six newly elected Democrats who belong to the Democratic Socialists of America are expected to join: Representatives-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Angela Gonzales-Torres of California; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania. The caucus also announced that Daniel Biss (IL-9), Bob Brooks (PA-7), Sam Forstag (MT-1) and Patty Garcia (IL-4) have joined, and more could be added to its roster. Leadership: Representative Greg Casar of Texas serves as chairman, with Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota as deputy chair. Vice chairs include Representatives Ro Khanna of California and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York serves on the executive board. Policy priorities: In April, the CPC unveiled a 10-part New Affordability Agenda that would lower household expenses through a combination of expanded government benefits, tighter corporate regulation, and new restrictions on the influence of wealthy donors. Its proposals include capping child care expenses at 7% of family income, providing $20,000 in down payment assistance to first-time homebuyers, expanding rental assistance and creating a government program to sell discounted generic prescription drugs. Other proposals would require companies to pay double wages for overtime, guarantee workers two weeks of paid vacation, and prohibit businesses from using personal data and artificial intelligence to determine what prices it charges consumers. The agenda also calls for taxing excess profits earned by oil companies and returning the proceeds to consumers, restricting what the caucus considers excessive utility charges and abolishing super PACs. What to watch: Although the caucus will remain smaller than the New Democrat Coalition, the arrival of newly elected democratic socialists could sharpen its demands of Democratic leadership. Several incoming lawmakers have already signaled that they intend to use their votes as leverage to secure commitments on issues like Medicare for All, defunding ICE, and ending American military assistance to Israel. The breadth of the CPC’s agenda could create both opportunities for cooperation and points of friction with the party's moderate wing. Both the New Democrats and progressives have identified affordability as a top priority, and their proposals overlap on housing construction, prescription drug costs, and corporate competition. But the groups differ over how aggressively the federal government should intervene. Blue Dog Coalition Estimated membership : 23 Overview : The Blue Dogs describe themselves as fiscally responsible Democrats committed to practical economic policies, national security, and the needs of communities that are sometimes overlooked by national party leaders, including rural and tribal areas. Once a major force in the party, the Blue Dogs are now one of the smallest ideological groups in the House. Members in the new Congress : The new class of Blue Dog Democrats includes Representatives-elect Johnny Garcia and Bobby Pulido of Texas, JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Jamie Ager and Paul Barringer of North Carolina, Sam Forstag of Montana, Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman of Wisconsin, Jake Johnson of Minnesota, Zach Dembo of Kentucky, Nancy Lacore of South Carolina, Bob Brooks of Pennsylvania, Zack Mullock of New Jersey, and Eileen Laubacher of Colorado. Many of the incoming members unseated Republican incumbents. Leadership: The coalition is led by three co-chairs: Representatives Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, and Lou Correa of California. Representative Adam Gray of California will serve as Blue Dog PAC Chair. Policy priorities: The Blue Dogs have traditionally emphasized fiscal discipline, government accountability, and a willingness to break with party leadership on issues important to their districts. What to watch: The Blue Dogs could become important voices in negotiations over federal spending, particularly if Democratic leaders seek Republican support for legislation. They could also exert influence over the party's political messaging, arguing that retaining control of the House in 2028 will depend on demonstrating that Democrats can govern effectively in districts where conservative voters remain a substantial part of the electorate. Bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus Estimated membership: Unknown. In the last Congress, it included 23 Democrats and 20 Republicans. Overview: Unlike the other three groups, the Problem Solvers Caucus is explicitly bipartisan, bringing together moderate Democrats and Republicans who favor negotiation and compromise as a way to advance legislation in an increasingly polarized Congress. Members in the new Congress: The caucus does not endorse candidates because of its bipartisan structure, and a list of incoming members has not been announced. Democrats retained 19 seats held by caucus members in the midterms, while Republicans lost 13 seats represented by members of the group. Leadership: Unknown. The past chairs were Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, a Republican who lost his seat, and Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who won re-election. Policy priorities: The caucus describes its mission as building relationships across party lines and identifying areas of agreement on major policy questions. Its members have generally sought to position themselves as pragmatic lawmakers willing to negotiate with the opposing party, even when doing so invites criticism from their own political bases. What to watch: While Democrats will control both chambers of Congress next year, Trump will remain in the White House, so any measure that reaches the President's desk will be subject to his veto. Most major bills will also still need Republican support to overcome the Senate filibuster. The Problem Solvers Caucus could play an important role in bridging those divides, particularly on issues such as health care and government funding.

items.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
items.summary: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024).

items.summary: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church.
